newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Bradford & Bingley boosts mutual benefits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bradford & Bingley boosts mutual benefits.

text.p: Mutually owned Bradford & Bingley Building Society on Wednesday doubled its members' benefit package to 100 million pounds ($159 million) a year.

The society, which has vehemently rejected the path of conversion to bank status accompanied by stock market flotation espoused by some other mutuals, said its benefits package had helped expand its business in 1996.

The home loan and savings society said the programme to distribute profits to members, which ran at one million pounds per week in 1996, had reduced annual profit after tax to 56.6 million pounds from 107.7 million in 1995.
At the same time, the society increased its assets by nearly nine percent to 17 billion pounds.

"In 1996 our asset growth was 50 percent above our natural market share and we expect that to continue -- it will be very hard for the soon-to-be banks to compete," finance director John Smith told Reuters.
Rather than converting, as rival home loan and savings organisations such as the Halifax and the Woolwich plan this year, Bradford & Bingley is committed to remaining a mutual.
Bradford & Bingley said its sole objective was to meet the needs of its members. It reduces profit levels by giving members lower mortgage interest rates and higher savings rates.

The first result of the increased distribution programme will be a "significant" across-the-board increase in savings rates, which will take effect from March 24, and at its annual meeting in April, the society will outline a new "loyalty package" to reward existing borrowers.
"Making lower profits than a Plc is not a problem for a mutual with substantial reserves. Indeed for a strong mutual, it is desirable," the society said in its results statement.

Bradford & Bingley chairman Lindsey Mackinley said in the statement, "With 900 million pounds ($1.4 billion) in reserves, the society is in good shape to meet the challenges which lie ahead. Our commitment to mutuality is unswerving."

Smith said this had resulted in mortgage rates 1/4 point below its rivals. Savings rates are harder to compare given the wide range of products, but Smith said its rates in general were better than those of the societies planning to convert.
Smith denied that converting societies might be able to attract higher quality new business -- for example from people to whom they would be able to sell other products.
"The most discerning customers will seek the best rates, so that should help the quality of the business," Smith said.

Operating profits in 1996 were affected by a 15 million pounds charge for the society's reorganisation and redundancy programme and a 20 million pounds reduction in pre-tax profit as a result of a more conservative accounting policy which takes into account the impact of mortgage incentives such as discounts and cashbacks.
The society's management expenses fell to 1.16 percent of mean assets from 1.19 percent, excluding the exceptional items, and it said it planned further reductions
Bad and doubtful debts dropped by 86 percent to 1.8 million stg, and the number of borrowers more than twelve months in arrears fell by 37 percent.

Smith echoed other industry comments on the UK housing market, saying it was showing signs of recovery but that this was not uniform, with London and south east England boosted by special factors such as an influx of people from Hong Kong.
"We think it (the market) will recover in 1997, but not boom away as it did in the '80s, which none of us want to see," he said. ($ = 0.628 British Pounds)
